newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Fake vodka kills Russians as genuine stuff rare.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Fake vodka kills Russians as genuine stuff rare.

text.p: Russia's battle against bootleg liquor has taken on new urgency following the death of at least 20 people in the Siberian city of Krasnoyarsk after drinking moonshine vodka.

Officials say the Krasnoyarsk incident, in which dozens of people were treated in hospital, is just a small example of a much larger problem. Many impoverished Russians seek cheap alcohol sold in thousands of tiny kiosks throughout the country, but the quality is often suspect.
"Fake vodka poisoning claims 50,000-100,000 lives of Russians a year. It is a real disaster, a genocide," said Vladimir Yarmosh, head of Russia's powerful alcohol producers' lobby Spirtprom.

"Traditional legal producers now control 24 percent of the Russian vodka market. Legal foreign imports account for about five percent. The rest is fake domestic poison or foreign contraband, most of which is dangerous as well."

Yarmosh's figures are higher than official statistics which show that alcohol poisoning accounted for almost 23 deaths per every 100,000 Russians in 1996 or about 35,000 people a year. But even the official rate is twice as high as it was in 1990.
Official figures show that an average Russian knocks back half a half-litre bottle of vodka each day.
Many people see a glass of vodka as an antidote to stress in the harsh new world of capitalism, but they try to save money by opting for cheaper but often dangerous brands.
Elderly women sell vodka from the cloth bags in underground passages, trying to make a few roubles to boost their miniscule pensions. Nobody knows where the vodka comes from.
The government has introduced licences and special labels to force the kiosks and street markets to clean up their act, but Yarmosh said the decrees had not made things much better.
"All those resolutions were issued in good faith to prevent thousands of deaths and to bolster weak state coffers. But they are not being fulfilled."
BLACK MARKET BOOZE BEATS THE TAXMAN
The health hazards posed by the moonshine are only part of Russia's vodka problem. Officials complain that the black market is depriving the treasury of much needed tax revenues.

Even taxed vodka is cheap by international standards -- a half-litre bottle costs around 22,000 roubles in Moscow ($3.8) -- but Yarmosh said more had to be done to bring in more tax and discourage drinking.

"Vodka has to be more expensive, it has to yield more to the budget and people do not have to buy it cheap," he said. "Tens of thousands die from simply drinking too much, not necessarily fake vodka. It should be too expensive for schoolkids."
Alcohol is potentially a huge source of government revenue.
Before the 1917 revolution which brought the Bolsheviks to power the tsars raked in about a third of Russia's overall income from alcohol. Now alcohol tax brings in just two percent.
Spirtprom officials said Russia made $1.55 from every bottle, compared to $9.37 in Sweden.

The State Tax Service, which views revenue from vodka sales as a way to plug an embarrassingly large hole in the budget, is predicting a rise in Russian vodka sales this year, with legal production set to double from 1996 to 1.7 billion litres in 1997.

Officials take comfort from a ban on the sale of strong alcoholic beverages except in walk-in stores. The ban, which takes effect on July 1, is aimed at taking on the grandmothers and Russia's popular but poorly regulated street kiosks.

Spirtprom officials said Russian distilleries only produced 202 million litres of vodka and 137 million litres of raw alcohol in January-April -- down 15 and 19 percent respectively from the same period last year.
RUSSIA'S BATTLE WITH THE BOTTLE
Russia has a long history of fighting its people's notorious drinking habits, but each ban led only to wider-scale alcohol consumption, propelled higher when the bans were scrapped.
The latest attempt dates back to the last years of the Soviet Union, when president Mikhail Gorbachev introduced harsh curbs on alcohol sales.

Consumption of sugar, used to make moonshine vodka, soared and gleaming stills steamed day and night to squeeze strong-smelling "samogon" or moonshine vodka from anything from grain to wood or potatoes. Thousands of people were poisoned.

The industry returned to normal in the early 1990s, but not for long. Production and sales of genuine Russian vodka slumped when Moscow allowed some charities to import certain goods, including alcohol and tobacco, tax-free.
The privileges were scrapped in 1996 after the market was flooded with cheap foreign brands, but Russia's beleaguered alcohol industry did not recover. Contraband and moonshine continued to flow.
Domestic vodka producers said legally produced vodka was the cheapest in the world, but it was still more expensive than illicit drink which is not subject to taxes and excise duties.

Last week they presented the government with a plan to sell cheap but good-quality "people's vodka" in a bid to elbow their way back into the domestic market and cope with a wave of vodka-related deaths.
"A two-thousand-rouble price difference ($0.40) makes a lot of difference for an average Russian, who makes $100 a month," said a senior industry official.
